content: Second language (L2) learners are a diverse group of individuals whose L2 skills vary significantly. These variations are influenced by internal factors, such as cognitive development, and external factors, such as cultural and linguistic environments. On average, L2 learners tend to have lower vocabulary skills in their second language compared to their monolingual peers. This disparity often persists over time and can negatively impact their social interactions, inclusion in society, learning processes, and academic performance. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the immediate and long-term effects of vocabulary interventions on L2 learners up to six years of age. Specifically, the review focused on how these interventions influence vocabulary acquisition and social-emotional well-being. Additionally, the review aimed to explore the relationships between the effectiveness of these interventions and the general characteristics of L2 learners, such as their age, exposure to the second language, and skills in their first language. To conduct this review, standard Cochrane search methods were employed, with the most recent search completed in December 2022. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared the effects of vocabulary interventions for L2 learners under six years old with standard care practices. The primary outcomes assessed were receptive L2 vocabulary (the ability to understand words), expressive L2 vocabulary (the ability to produce words), and mean length of utterance (MLU), which was used as a measure of potential adverse effects. Secondary outcomes included L2 narrative skills, receptive and expressive vocabulary in the first language (L1), L1 listening comprehension, L2 grammatical knowledge, L2 reading comprehension in the long term, and socio-emotional well-being, as measured by the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire. The review identified 12 studies involving a total of 1,943 participants. These studies were conducted in various countries, including Norway, the USA, Canada, China, and the Netherlands. Most of the studies (10 out of 12) were carried out in preschool settings, with preschool teachers typically delivering the interventions. The interventions were often conducted in small groups of three to four children, with an average weekly duration of 80 minutes, ranging from 24 to 120 minutes. A common approach used in these interventions was shared book reading, where target vocabulary words were embedded within the books being read aloud to the children. The standard care provided to comparison groups varied depending on the local context and preschool settings. The effects of L2 vocabulary interventions, compared to standard care, varied depending on the outcome measures. For vocabulary outcomes that included words explicitly taught during the intervention (proximal outcomes), the interventions had a large effect on both receptive vocabulary (standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.97, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.64 to 1.30; 4 studies, 1,973 participants; very low-certainty evidence) and expressive vocabulary (SMD 0.86, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.17; 6 studies, 1,121 participants; very low-certainty evidence). However, the confidence in these results was limited due to concerns about bias, substantial variability between studies, and wide confidence intervals. For vocabulary outcomes that did not include words explicitly taught during the intervention (distal outcomes), the effects were smaller. The interventions had a small effect on receptive vocabulary (SMD 0.29, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.55; 6 studies, 1,074 participants; low-certainty evidence) and likely had little to no effect on expressive vocabulary (SMD 0.10, 95% CI −0.02 to 0.23; 7 studies, 960 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). There was little to no effect on L2 listening comprehension (SMD 0.19, 95% CI −0.31 to 0.68; 2 studies, 294 participants; very low-certainty evidence), though the evidence was uncertain. The interventions likely resulted in a slight improvement in L2 narrative skills (SMD 0.37, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.59; 2 studies, 487 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). Only one study reported data on mean length of utterance (MLU), so the effect of the intervention on this outcome could not be thoroughly examined. The evidence regarding socio-emotional well-being was insufficient to draw conclusions. Additionally, due to a lack of data, the planned subgroup analyses to explore the relationships between intervention effects and learner characteristics could not be conducted. In conclusion, the findings of this review suggest that vocabulary interventions may enhance L2 vocabulary acquisition in young children compared to standard care. However, these interventions appear to have little to no effect on listening comprehension, and the evidence for this outcome is uncertain. Vocabulary interventions may slightly improve storytelling skills. Given the limited number of studies that met the inclusion criteria and the low to moderate certainty of the evidence due to inconsistency and imprecision, these findings should be interpreted with caution. The review underscores the need for more high-quality randomized controlled trials, particularly those conducted outside the USA, to better understand the effects of vocabulary interventions for L2 learners.
